newsitem.title: USA: Union "not that far apart" from American.
newsitem.headline: Union "not that far apart" from American.

text.p: An American Airlines pilots union spokesman said the two sides were "not that far apart" on terms for a new contract to avert a strike set for midnight Friday at the nation's No. 2 carrier.
The union also said it made a new proposal on pay in the contract dispute.
Allied Pilots Association spokesman Wally Pitts told reporters it was possible to reach an agreement and head off the threatened strike. "We're not that far apart," Pitts said.

The threat of a walkout at the huge airline has raised fears for thousands of travelers, resorts and others who could suffer financially if American is grounded, raising the possibility the White House might become involved.
The union's chief negotiator, Brian Mayhew, said the proposal was made late Wednesday during joint negotiations with American.
"We have been working that issue through the (federal) mediation board," which is overseeing the negotiations, Mayhew added. Another union spokesman said there had been no response from American.
The pay proposal was the latest in a series of offers by the airline and the union.

The union had proposed an 11.5 percent pay increase over four years, with American countering with 4 percent. Earlier this week, American increased its offer to 6 percent, but withdrew one of two stock options it previously included.
The pilots rejected the 6 percent offer and the withdrawal of the second stock option, saying its overall effect was a package reduced in value by $43.1 million.
The most contentious issues between the union and American are pay and which pilots would fly the new smaller jets the airline intends to buy for its regional airline, American Eagle.

American wants to have lower-paid Eagle pilots from another union fly them, while the Allied Pilots Association wants its members to fly the aircraft. American has said it needed the lower-paid pilots in order to be competitive with other major carriers which have low-cost regional airline services.

The union late last night made another proposal under which it would accept lower pay for its members who would fly the smaller jets, provided the jets flew under the "American Airlines" banner and not that of Eagle.
But an American Airlines spokesman Thursday dismissed that offer, calling it "a bunch of verbiage on paper.
Union spokesmen said they remained frustrated at the pace of the talks, saying "the clock is ticking."
